newsitem.title: USA: U.S. pledges $7.3 million in relief for Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pledges $7.3 million in relief for Iraq.

text.p: The United States, after an initial cool reaction to a U.N. appeal, on Wednesday offered $7.3 million in emergency aid for Iraqi civilians but blamed Saddam Hussein for wasting billions of dollars while his people go hungry.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, in announcing the aid, said the U.S. donation would come with a caveat -- that the money be used only for Kurds in northern Iraq.

That region was effectively a "safe haven" -- patrolled by U.S., French and British warplanes -- until rival Kurdish factions recently unleashed civil war there. The air patrols continue but relief and other programmes have been disrupted.

U.N. relief agencies said on Monday thousands of people were threatened by lack of food, medicine and clean water in Iraq, partly due to U.N. sanctions imposed on Baghdad since its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The sanctions ban Iraqi oil exports but allow humanitarian supplies.

At a news conference in New York, agency officials estimated that 4,500 children were dying monthly and they complained that few countries had responded to their appeal for $40 million in new relief assistance.

That day, the State Department reacted cooly to the news conference with Burns saying Washington had no way of evaluating "the degree of the crisis" in Iraq because it had no diplomats on the ground there.

Besides, the "way to correct the problem of Iraqi malnutrition ... and deprivation on the part of Iraqi citizens (is) for (Iraqi leader) Saddam Hussein to start caring about what happens to his people, instead of building 15 palaces, enriching his family with overseas bank accounts," Burns said.

On Tuesday, howvever, the spokesman made a point of stressing deep concern over reports that thousands of Iraqis were at risk this winter due to lack of essential goods, although he continued to blame Saddam for the crisis.
On Wednesday Burns announced that "we do intend to contribute $7.3 million with a caveat that this money be used to assist the Kurds in northern Iraq."
The contribution will go through the U.N. World Food Programme, and Burns said he was confident the U.S. condition regarding the Kurds could be worked out.
"We are sympathetic to the people of Iraq who are the victims of Saddam Hussein" and believe other countries should also contribute to the U.N. relief aid appeal, he said.

Although he previously raised doubts about the "degree of crisis" in Iraq and some data the aid agencies drew upon for their assessments, Burns said on Wednesday: "We do have faith in the World Food Programme and UNICEF (United Nations Children's Fund). They're credible organisations."

"No one, I think ... in either of those organisations or in this government can tell you exactly how many children are at risk in Iraq. But we know enough about Iraq to know that conditions there are appalling ... And we have a humanitarian responsibility and we'll act on it," he said.
But Burns continued to hold Saddam responsible for the crisis.

He reiterated U.S. charges that since 1992 the Iraqi leader spent upwards of $2 billion for 48 palaces, plus millions more rebuilding his army, maintaining a presidential yacht and feathering personal offshore bank accounts.

"He's responsible. He's the leader of Iraq. If people are starving in his country ... look where the money trail is with Saddam Hussein," Burns said, adding: "He's letting children die because he prefers to build palaces to himself. He prefers to put millions of dollars into bank accounts for his children -- his own children."
